label: Geodesics
notes: Welcome to Chapter 20, printed pages 366 through 378. A geodesic is the surface analogue of a straight line: the curve a taut thread traces on a surface, locally shortest and never bending sideways within the surface. We build that intuition first, then make it precise through geodesic curvature and the geodesic equations.

label: Straightest and Shortest
notes: We open with the two complementary definitions a geodesic satisfies at once. Pull a thread tight on a globe and it lies along the straightest available track while also minimizing length locally. Holding both pictures together prevents the common error of treating geodesics as merely globally shortest paths, which they are not in general.

label: Geodesic Curvature
notes: Here we decompose the curvature vector of a surface curve into a normal part absorbed by the surface and a tangential part, the geodesic curvature kappa-g. This single scalar measures sideways bending felt within the surface. Emphasize that kappa-g is intrinsic: it depends only on the first fundamental form, not on how the surface sits in space.

label: Zero Geodesic Curvature
notes: This is the defining property of a geodesic: its geodesic curvature vanishes identically, so the principal normal of the curve coincides with the surface normal. All bending is forced by the surface itself. We contrast a geodesic with a latitude circle, whose curvature has a stubborn tangential component, so it bends within the surface.

label: The Geodesic Equations
notes: We derive the geodesic equations as the Euler-Lagrange conditions for stationary arc length. The Christoffel symbols of the first fundamental form encode how coordinate directions twist, and the equations say the acceleration has no tangential component. Stress that this is a second-order ODE: a starting point and direction determine a unique geodesic.

label: Geodesic Polar Form
notes: We specialize the metric to geodesic polar coordinates, ds-squared equals dr-squared plus f of r squared d-theta-squared. The radial function f carries all the geometry: angular momentum f-squared theta-prime is conserved along any geodesic, and curvature is minus f-double-prime over f. This compact template recurs through the rest of the chapter.

label: Great Circles on the Sphere
notes: The flagship example: every geodesic of a sphere is a great circle, the intersection with a plane through the center. We contrast the short great-circle arc joining two cities with a latitude circle between the same points, which looks direct on a flat map but is genuinely longer. This is why flight paths bow poleward.

label: Clairaut's Theorem
notes: On any surface of revolution, the product r times sine psi stays constant along a geodesic, where r is distance from the axis and psi the angle the geodesic makes with the meridian. We read this as conservation of angular momentum. As a geodesic climbs toward a thinner part of the surface, psi must grow to compensate.

label: Clairaut on a Surface of Revolution
notes: Here we visualize Clairaut's relation directly. A geodesic winds around a vase-shaped surface; at the wide waist psi is small, and near the narrow neck where r shrinks, sine psi swells toward one until the geodesic grazes a barrier circle and turns back. The constant r sine psi sets that turning radius precisely.

label: Cylinder and Cone
notes: Developable surfaces make geodesics easy: unroll them flat and geodesics become ordinary straight lines. On a cylinder the unrolled lines wind back into helices; on a cone they become straight segments that can self-intersect after unwrapping. We use this to reinforce that geodesics are intrinsic, surviving any bending that does not stretch the surface.

label: Triangles and Total Curvature
notes: We connect geodesics to curvature in the large. The integral of Gaussian curvature over a geodesic triangle equals its angle sum minus pi: excess on the sphere, defect in the hyperbolic plane. Summing such budgets over a closed surface cancels interior edges and yields the Gauss-Bonnet relation, total curvature equals two pi times the Euler characteristic.

label: Recap and Constant Curvature
notes: We close by tying the thread together: zero geodesic curvature, the Euler-Lagrange equations, great circles, and Clairaut's invariant all describe one object. The radial template with f equal to sin r, r, or sinh r packages spherical, flat, and hyperbolic geometry uniformly, and the pseudosphere reminds us a constant-negative-curvature surface need not hold the whole hyperbolic plane.
